Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 1:

﴿To bring mankind out of darkness into light﴾ The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). "Darknesses" (al-zulumat) are disbelief (kufr) and ignorance (jahl), and "light" (al-nur) is faith (iman) and knowledge (ilm). ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾ i.e., by His command, which is His sending (of the Messenger). ﴿To the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "to the light."

Allah (﴿اللَّهُ﴾): it is read in the nominative (raf'), in which case it is a subject (mubtada') or the predicate of a hidden subject; and in the genitive (khafd), in which case it is an apposition (badal) to ﴿يَسْتَحِبُّونَ﴾, meaning "they prefer." ﴿وَيَبْغُونَهَا﴾ ("and they seek it crooked"): this has already been explained. ﴿بِلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ﴾ means in the language and speech of his people. ﴿أَنْ أَخْرِجْ﴾ ("that bring out"): the "an" (أن) is either explanatory (mufassirah) or verbal-masdar (masdariyyah) with the implied sense of "bi-an" (that). ﴿وَذَكِّرْهُمْ بِأَيَّامِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("and remind them of the days of Allah"): that is, His punishments upon the earlier nations. It was also said: His bounties upon the Children of Israel. The wording encompasses both blessings and retributions. The days are described as "days" (ayyam) because they occurred in days, and in this there is an exalting of them, like the saying "such a day and such a day."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 6–7:

﴿And they slaughter your sons﴾. It is mentioned here with the conjunction "wa" (and), to indicate that the evil torment is other than the slaughtering, or more general than that, and then the slaughtering is singled out (for mention), like His saying: ﴿And His angels and Jibril and Mika'il﴾. In al-Baqarah it is mentioned without "wa", as an explanation of the torment. ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ is from the speech of Musa. Ta'adhdhana (proclaimed) means adhana (announced), i.e., made known, like your saying: tawa'ada and awa'ada (both meaning "threatened"). Allah's making known is accompanied by the carrying out of what He has made known. ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾: this is the object of ta'adhdhana, because it includes the meaning of "qala" (said). The increase may be in worldly good, or in reward in the Hereafter, or in both. ﴿But if you are ungrateful﴾: it may mean that He intends the ingratitude for blessings (kufr al-ni'am), or disbelief in faith (al-kufr bil-iman); the first is more preferred because it is contrasted with gratitude (al-shukr).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 8–10:

﴿لاَ يَعْلَمُهُمْ إِلاَّ ٱللَّهُ﴾ is an expression for their great number, like His saying: ﴿وَقُرُوناً بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ كَثِيراً﴾ [al-Furqan: 38] (﴿And generations between them, many﴾).

﴿فَرَدُّوۤاْ أَيْدِيَهُمْ فِيۤ أَفْوَٰهِهِمْ﴾ (﴿But they put their hands over their mouths﴾). There are three opinions on this. The first is that the pronouns refer to the people of the messengers, and the meaning is that they put their hands into their own mouths out of rage against the messengers, like His saying: ﴿عضوا عليكم الأنامل من الغيظ﴾ (they bite their fingertips at you out of rage), or out of mockery and laughter, like one overcome by laughter who places his hand over his mouth. The second is that the pronouns refer to them (the disbelievers), and the meaning is that they put their hands into their own mouths, gesturing to the prophets to be silent. The third is that they put their hands into the mouths of the prophets to silence them and to reject their words ﴿أَفِي ٱللَّهِ شَكٌّ﴾ (﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾). The meaning is: is there doubt about the existence of God, or about His divinity? It was said: about His oneness. The hamza here is for affirmation and rebuke, because it does not admit doubt due to the clarity of the proofs; for this reason He described Him afterwards by saying: ﴿فَاطِرِ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلأَرْضِ﴾ (﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾).

﴿مِّن ذُنُوبِكُمْ﴾ (﴿of your sins﴾). It was said: min (مِن) here is extra (zaʾida). Sibawayh rejected its being extra in an affirmative sentence, and in his view it is for partition (lil-tab'īḍ). The meaning is that when the disbeliever embraces Islam, what preceded his sin before Islam is forgiven, while what he sins after it remains subject to God's will. Thus forgiveness falls on a part. No forgiveness of some sins is mentioned in the Qur'an except for the disbeliever, as in this place; and what is in al-Ahqaf and Surat Nuh, and it comes for believers without min, as in al-Saff.

﴿وَيُؤَخِّرَكُمْ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍ مُّسَـمًّـى﴾ (﴿and defer you to a specified term﴾). al-Zamakhshari and the people of his school among the Mu'tazila said: the meaning is that He will defer you, if you believe, to your appointed terms; and if you do not believe, He will hasten you to destruction before that time. This is based on their view of two terms (al-ajalayn), and the People of the Sunna reject this, for the term according to them is one and fixed.

﴿قَالُوۤاْ إِنْ أَنتُمْ إِلاَّ بَشَرٌ مِّثْلُنَا﴾ (﴿They said: You are only human beings like us﴾). It may be that their saying is a denial of the preference of some humans over others through prophethood, or it may be a rejection of the prophethood of a human being. The first is more apparent, due to their demand for proof in their saying: ﴿فَأْتُونَا بِسُلْطَانٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾ (﴿so bring us a clear authority﴾), and the saying of the messengers: ﴿وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَمُنُّ عَلَىٰ مَن يَشَآءُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ﴾ (﴿but God bestows His favor upon whom He wills of His servants﴾), i.e., by preferring them with prophethood.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verses 12–13:

﴿And why should we not put our trust in Allah?﴾ The meaning: what prevents us from putting our trust in Allah? ﴿And we will surely bear with patience whatever harm you inflict upon us. And upon Allah let those who rely (upon Him) put their trust.﴾ If it is asked, why was the command repeated? My answer is that His saying, "And upon Allah let the believers put their trust," refers back to what preceded, namely the demand of the disbelievers for "a clear authority" (sultan mubin), that is, a manifest proof. So the trust of the messengers in facing it is in Allah. As for His saying, "let those who rely (upon Him) put their trust," it refers back to their saying, "and we will surely bear with patience whatever harm you inflict upon us," meaning: we will rely upon Allah in repelling your harm.

Al-Zamakhshari said: this second [command] carries the sense of steadfastness in trust (al-thubut 'ala al-tawakkul). ﴿Or you will surely return to our religion.﴾ The "aw" (or) here means "illa an" (except that), or it retains its original sense, indicating that one of the two things will occur. The "return" ('awd) here means "becoming" (al-sayratu), which is frequent in the speech of the Arabs, and it does not imply that the messengers were previously in the religion of the disbelievers.

﴿Khāfa maqāmī﴾ (﴿those who fear My standing [before Me]﴾). There are three interpretations of this, here and in ﴿And for him who fears the standing [before] his Lord there are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. The first is that it means the station of reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. The second is that it means God's watchful standing over His servants with respect to their deeds. The third is that it means "he feared Me and feared his Lord," with maqām either being superfluous (iqhām) or being used to refer to the Essence (al-dhāt).

"And they sought victory" — the pronoun refers to the messengers, i.e., they sought help from God. Its root meaning is seeking an opening (fath), which is judgment (hukm). ﴿every obstinate tyrant﴾ — i.e., one who is overbearing (qahir) or arrogant (mutakabbir). ﴿obstinate﴾ — one who opposes submission. ﴿Behind him﴾ — in both places; here "al-wara'" (behind) means what lies ahead in time, and it was said that its meaning here is "in front of him," and this is far-fetched. ﴿and he will be made to drink﴾ — coordinated with an omitted element, whose implied sense is: "Behind him is Hell, into which he will be cast and made to drink." This drinking is mentioned separately after the mention of Hell because it is among the most severe of its torments. ﴿He will gulp it down, yet he will hardly swallow it﴾ — i.e., he will force himself to gulp it, and swallowing it will be difficult for him. The negation with "kada" (hardly/barely) implies that swallowing occurs only after great effort. The meaning of "yusighuhu" is that he swallows it. ﴿Death will come to him from every place﴾ — i.e., he will find the water like the pain and anguish of death from all directions. ﴿Yet he will not die﴾ — i.e., he will not find relief through death.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 18:

﴿The parable of those who disbelieved﴾ The view of Sibawayh (the grammarian) and al-Farra' (al-Farra') regarding it is like their view concerning "the parable of the Garden which is promised" in Surah al-Ra'd and al-Qital (Surah Muhammad). According to Sibawayh, the predicate is omitted, its estimated sense being: "what is recited to you." According to al-Farra', the predicate is the clause that follows it. The word "mathal" here means "likeness" (shabih). ﴿Their deeds are like ashes﴾ comparing them to ashes in their vanishing and disappearance. ﴿on a stormy day﴾ i.e., a day of strong wind; and "'usuf" (violent blowing) in reality is an attribute of the wind. ﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ i.e., they see no benefit from it.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 21:**

﴿And they will come forth before Allah﴾ means they will become manifest. The manifestation here is their emergence from the graves. It was also said: it means they became in the open (al-biraz), which is the wide, expansive land. ﴿Tabi'an﴾ is the plural of tabi' (follower), or a verbal noun (masdar) used as a description with intensive force (balagha), or it is according to an omitted modifier (hadhf mudaf), i.e., "ones who followed." ﴿From the punishment of Allah, anything﴾: the first "min" (from) is explanatory (li al-bayan), and the second "min" (some of) is partitive (li al-tab'id). It is permissible that both are partitive together, as said by al-Zamakhshari. The more evident view is that the first is explanatory and the second is extra (za'idah), and the meaning is: "Will you bear off from us or take on for us anything of the punishment of Allah?" ﴿A place of escape﴾ means a refuge (mahrab) wherever it occurs; it may be a verbal noun (masdar) or a noun of place (ism makan).

﴿And Satan will say﴾: meaning Iblis al-Aqdam (the Ancient One). It is reported that he will stand up to deliver this speech on the Day of Resurrection, or in the Fire, saying it to its people. ﴿When the matter has been decided﴾: if Iblis's speech is on the Day of Resurrection, then the meaning of "the matter has been decided" (qudiya al-amr) is that a group has been assigned to the Fire and a group to the Garden. If it is in the Fire, then the meaning of "the matter has been decided" is that the people of the Fire have come to be in the Fire and the people of the Garden in the Garden. ﴿Except that I called you﴾: this is a munqati' (disconnected) exception. ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾: meaning, I cannot be your rescuer, nor can you be rescuers for me. ﴿For your associating me﴾: here mā is a masdariyya (verbal-noun particle), meaning: because of your associating me with God in obedience. ﴿Before﴾: this is connected to "you associated" (ashraktumūn). It may also be connected to "you disbelieved" (kafartum), but the first is clearer and more preferable. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers﴾: this is a resumption (i'nāf) from the speech of God Most High, and it may be a report of Iblis's words. ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾: this is connected to "will enter" (udkhila) or to "abiding therein" (khālidīna). The first is better.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 24–27:

﴿A good word﴾ [qāla] Ibn ʿAbbās and others said it is: "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh). It was also said: every good deed. ﴿Like a good tree﴾ is the date palm according to the majority of scholars, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya chose that it is an unspecified tree, provided that it possesses those qualities. ﴿Its branches are in the sky﴾ meaning in the air, and this is an expression of its height. ﴿It yields its fruit at every season﴾. The word ḥīn (season) in the language denotes an unspecified period of time, though it may be accompanied by an indicator that limits it. It was said: "at every season" means every year, because the date palm bears fruit every year; and it was said other than that. ﴿And the likeness of an evil word﴾ is the word of disbelief, and it was said: every ugly word. ﴿Like an evil tree﴾ is the colocynth (ḥanẓal) according to the majority of scholars, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya chose that it is unspecified. ﴿Uprooted﴾ meaning pulled up, and the true meaning of ijtithāth is taking away the body (juththa), and this is in contrast to His saying: "Its root is firm." ﴿With the firm word﴾ is "There is no god but Allah" and the affirmation of prophethood. ﴿In the life of this world﴾ meaning: when they are tested, they do not waver. ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾ is, according to the majority, at the time of questioning in the grave.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 28–34:

﴿They have exchanged the favour of Allah for ingratitude﴾ The favour of Allah here is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his religion, which Allah bestowed upon the Quraysh, but they denied the favour and did not accept it. The implied meaning is: they exchanged the thanks due for the favour of Allah for ingratitude. ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of perdition﴾ That is, those who obeyed them and followed them. ﴿The abode of perdition﴾ He explained it by His words: Hell. ﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish the prayer and spend﴾ This is the answer to a condition, which is implied in His words "say" (qul). Its implied meaning is: if you tell them, "Establish [the prayer], and they will establish it." The object of the verb "say" on this reading is omitted. It has also been said that it is in the jussive mood through the implied imperative lam, meaning: "let them establish the prayer." ﴿Nor is there friendship﴾ From khullah (ikhlah), which is affection. ﴿Indeed, mankind﴾ He means the human species.

Surah 14, verses 35–36:

﴿the city safe﴾ mentioned in al-Baqarah [2:125]. ﴿Keep me and my sons away﴾: i.e., preserve me. Its past tense is janaba, and it is said janaba and jannaba (with the intensive form), and ajnaba carry the same meaning. ﴿and my sons﴾: meaning my own offspring, and among them his prayer was answered. As for the descendants of his sons, they worshipped idols. ﴿and whoever disobeys me﴾: meaning whoever disobeyed him by committing a sin other than disbelief, and by committing disbelief and then repenting from it; this is the one for whom it is correct to pray for forgiveness. However, he mentioned the wording in general terms because of the mercy he (peace be upon him) had towards creation and his excellent character.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verses 37–38:

﴿I have settled some of my offspring﴾ meaning his son Isma'il (peace be upon him). When his mother Hajar gave birth to him, Sarah, the wife of Ibrahim, became jealous of her, so he took him along with his mother from al-Sham to Makkah, ﴿in a valley﴾ meaning Makkah. A wadi (valley) is the land between two mountains, even if there is no water in it. ﴿Near Your Sacred House﴾ meaning the Ka'bah. Either the House existed before Ibrahim, as is reported in some narrations, or Ibrahim knew that he would build a House there. ﴿That they may establish prayer﴾: the lam here may be the lam of command, meaning a supplication, or the lam of purpose (kay), in which case it is connected to "I have settled." The plural pronoun indicates that he knew his son would have descendants there. ﴿Make hearts among the people incline toward them﴾: that is, make them travel with determination and haste. Because of this supplication, God made the pilgrimage to the House beloved to people. The word "min" in "min al-nas" (among the people) is partitive. Some said: If he had said "af'idat al-nas" (the hearts of the people), Persia and the Romans would have performed the pilgrimage. ﴿And provide them with fruits﴾: that is, provide for them in that valley, even though it is not a place of cultivation. God answered his supplication and made the fruits of everything be brought to Makkah. ﴿And nothing is hidden from God﴾ (the verse): it may be part of the speech of God Most High, or a report of what Ibrahim said.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verses 39–40:

﴿Praise be to God, who has granted me, in my old age, Isma'il and Ishaq.﴾ It is related that Isma'il was born to him when he was one hundred and seventeen years old, and it is related that it was less than this. Isma'il was older than Ishaq. ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ If by "supplication" (du'a') is meant request and desire, then "acceptance" (qabul) means response (istijaba). If by "supplication" is meant worship (ibada), then "acceptance" is in its literal sense.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verses 41–43:

﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾. It was said that he prayed for forgiveness for his disbelieving parents only on condition of their becoming Muslim. The sound view, however, is that he prayed for them before it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of Allah, as is related in Surat Bara'ah. ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware﴾. This is a warning to the wrongdoers, who are the disbelievers according to the most apparent view. If it is asked: to whom is this address directed here, and in His saying: "So do not think that Allah will fail to fulfil His promise to His messengers"? The answer is that it may be addressed to the Prophet ﷺ or to someone else. If it is addressed to someone else, there is no difficulty. If it is addressed to him, it is problematic, because the Prophet ﷺ would not think that Allah is unaware. This is interpreted in two ways: the first is that what is meant is steadfastness upon his knowledge that Allah is not unaware and does not fail to fulfil His promise; the second is that what is meant is informing him of the punishment of the wrongdoers, so the purpose of the statement is a warning to them. ﴿Their eyes will stare fixedly﴾, i.e., the eyes will be fixed in gaze out of fear. ﴿Hastening forward﴾. It was said: al-Ih'ta' (ihtaʿ) is hastening, and it was said: it is an intense gaze without blinking. ﴿Raising their heads﴾. It was said: al-Iqna' (iqnaʿ) is raising the head, and it was said: lowering it out of humiliation. ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾, i.e., they will not blink their eyes out of dread and anguish.

﴿And their hearts will be a void﴾, i.e., confused and heedless, not comprehending anything because of the intensity of their anguish; it is likened to air in its lack of substance among things. It may also mean that their hearts will be agitated within their breasts.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verses 41–43:

﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾. It was said that he prayed for forgiveness for his disbelieving parents only on condition of their becoming Muslim. The sound view, however, is that he prayed for them before it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of Allah, as is related in Surat Bara'ah. ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware﴾. This is a warning to the wrongdoers, who are the disbelievers according to the most apparent view. If it is asked: to whom is this address directed here, and in His saying: "So do not think that Allah will fail to fulfil His promise to His messengers"? The answer is that it may be addressed to the Prophet ﷺ or to someone else. If it is addressed to someone else, there is no difficulty. If it is addressed to him, it is problematic, because the Prophet ﷺ would not think that Allah is unaware. This is interpreted in two ways: the first is that what is meant is steadfastness upon his knowledge that Allah is not unaware and does not fail to fulfil His promise; the second is that what is meant is informing him of the punishment of the wrongdoers, so the purpose of the statement is a warning to them. ﴿Their eyes will stare fixedly﴾, i.e., the eyes will be fixed in gaze out of fear. ﴿Hastening forward﴾. It was said: al-Ih'ta' (ihtaʿ) is hastening, and it was said: it is an intense gaze without blinking. ﴿Raising their heads﴾. It was said: al-Iqna' (iqnaʿ) is raising the head, and it was said: lowering it out of humiliation. ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾, i.e., they will not blink their eyes out of dread and anguish.

﴿And their hearts will be a void﴾, i.e., confused and heedless, not comprehending anything because of the intensity of their anguish; it is likened to air in its lack of substance among things. It may also mean that their hearts will be agitated within their breasts.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 44:

﴿On the Day the punishment comes to them﴾ — meaning the Day of Resurrection. The accusative of "yawm" (day) is because it is the second object of "andhir" (warn), and it is not permissible for it to be an adverbial of time (zarf).

﴿Did you not used to swear﴾ — its estimated sense: it will be said to them, "Did you not used to swear," and so on, to the end of the verse.

﴿that you would have no cessation?﴾ — this is what was sworn to. The meaning of "min zawal" (from cessation) is: from the earth after death; that is, you swore that you would not be resurrected.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verses 46–47:

﴿And their plotting was with Allah﴾, i.e., the recompense of their plotting. ﴿And though their plotting was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾. Here "in" (in) is negating (nafiyah), the lam is the lam of denial (lam al-juhud), and "the mountains" is intended to mean the sacred laws (shara'i') and the prophethoods (nubuwwat), which are likened to mountains in their firmness. The meaning is: their plotting, since those firm, established mountains will not be moved by it. Al-Kisa'i read "li-tazula" with a fatha on the lam and a raf' (nominative) on "tazulu," and "in" in this reading is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqilah), with the lam serving for emphasis. The meaning is the magnification of their plotting, i.e., that because of its severity the mountains would be moved by it, but Allah protected and preserved [the sacred laws] from it. ﴿So do not think that Allah would break His promise to His messengers﴾, meaning the promise of victory over the disbelievers. If it is said: why did he not say "breaking His messengers His promise," and why was the second object placed before the first? The answer is that He placed the promise first to show that He does not break a promise at all, in any absolute sense. Then He said "His messengers" to show that if He does not break the promise of any of mankind, how then would He break the promise to His messengers and the choicest of His creation? So He placed the promise first with the intention of generality, then mentioned the messengers with the intention of specification.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verse 48:

﴿On the day the earth is changed into another earth﴾. The element governing the adverbial phrase (al-'amil fi al-zarf, the word that governs the time expression) is ﴿ذو انتقام﴾ ("the Mighty, the Lord of Retribution"), or it is an omitted verb. The changing of the earth on the Day of Resurrection means that it becomes white and pure, like a loaf of fine bread (كقرصة النقي), as is related in the authentic hadith (prophetic tradition). ﴿And the heavens﴾: their change is by being split open, the scattering of their stars, and the eclipsing of their sun and moon. It has also been said: the earth will be changed into silver and the heavens into gold, but this view is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 14, verses 49–52:

﴿And you will see the criminals﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿bound together in shackles﴾, i.e., tied up in chains. ﴿Their garments﴾, i.e., their shirts, and al-sarabil (garment) means a shirt, ﴿of tar﴾. It is connected to an omitted element, meaning that God placed this in them. It is the substance with which camels are coated for mange, and fire has a fierce blaze in it; therefore God made the shirts of the people of the Fire from it. ﴿So that God may recompense﴾ is connected to an omitted element, meaning God did that so that He may recompense. ﴿This is a message﴾ refers to the Qur'an or to what this surah contains. ﴿And that they may be warned﴾ is conjoined to an omitted element, whose sense is: so that they may be advised by it and warned. ﴿And that those of understanding may take heed﴾, i.e., this reminder is for people of intellect, and they are the people of knowledge, may God be pleased with them.
